Change of Variables

Stretch and squeeze the axis to rewrite an integral. Two different substitutions land on the same value.

Change the scale and the endpoints move along. Areas need correcting by the stretch factor. After the correction, a hard integral turns easy.

For example, measure with a 📏 ruler whose marks are stretched twofold and every reading doubles. Halving the reading corrects it back to the true length.

Examples & Exercises

Prove the substitution rule completely: if φ\varphiφ is C1C^1C1 and monotone on [a,b][a,b][a,b] and fff is continuous, then ∫abf(φ(x)) φ′(x) dx=∫φ(a)φ(b)f(u) du\int_a^b f(\varphi(x))\,\varphi'(x)\,dx = \int_{\varphi(a)}^{\varphi(b)} f(u)\,du∫ab​f(φ(x))φ′(x)dx=∫φ(a)φ(b)​f(u)du.

Take an antiderivative FFF with F′=fF' = fF′=f and apply the chain rule plus the fundamental theorem to F∘φF \circ \varphiF∘φ.

∫abf(φ(x)) φ′(x) dx=∫φ(a)φ(b)f(u) du\int_a^b f(\varphi(x))\,\varphi'(x)\,dx = \int_{\varphi(a)}^{\varphi(b)} f(u)\,du∫ab​f(φ(x))φ′(x)dx=∫φ(a)φ(b)​f(u)du
ddx[F(φ(x))]=F′(φ(x)) φ′(x)=f(φ(x)) φ′(x)\frac{d}{dx}\bigl[F(\varphi(x))\bigr] = F'(\varphi(x))\,\varphi'(x) = f(\varphi(x))\,\varphi'(x)dxd​[F(φ(x))]=F′(φ(x))φ′(x)=f(φ(x))φ′(x)
Show proof

  1. Since fff is continuous on an interval containing φ([a,b])\varphi([a,b])φ([a,b]), an antiderivative FFF with F′=fF' = fF′=f exists (a continuous function has one via integration). The composition H(x)=F(φ(x))H(x) = F(\varphi(x))H(x)=F(φ(x)) is C1C^1C1, and the chain rule gives H′(x)=F′(φ(x)) φ′(x)=f(φ(x)) φ′(x)H'(x) = F'(\varphi(x))\,\varphi'(x) = f(\varphi(x))\,\varphi'(x)H′(x)=F′(φ(x))φ′(x)=f(φ(x))φ′(x) — exactly the pre-substitution integrand.

  2. H′H'H′ is continuous, hence integrable on [a,b][a,b][a,b], and the FTC gives ∫abf(φ(x)) φ′(x) dx=∫abH′(x) dx=H(b)−H(a)=F(φ(b))−F(φ(a))\int_a^b f(\varphi(x))\,\varphi'(x)\,dx = \int_a^b H'(x)\,dx = H(b) - H(a) = F(\varphi(b)) - F(\varphi(a))∫ab​f(φ(x))φ′(x)dx=∫ab​H′(x)dx=H(b)−H(a)=F(φ(b))−F(φ(a)).

  3. Meanwhile the same FTC applied directly to fff gives ∫φ(a)φ(b)f(u) du=F(φ(b))−F(φ(a))\int_{\varphi(a)}^{\varphi(b)} f(u)\,du = F(\varphi(b)) - F(\varphi(a))∫φ(a)φ(b)​f(u)du=F(φ(b))−F(φ(a)) (monotonicity of φ\varphiφ guarantees φ(a)≤φ(b)\varphi(a) \le \varphi(b)φ(a)≤φ(b) or the reverse, so the interval is well-defined).

    Both sides agree, proving the substitution rule.

    Complete. (Tao 11.10.5–11.10.7.)

Compute ∫012x ex2 dx=e−1\int_0^1 2x\,e^{x^2}\,dx = e - 1∫01​2xex2dx=e−1 completely via the substitution u=x2u = x^2u=x2: determine dududu, transform the limits, and write out the antiderivative — no skipped steps.

∫012x ex2 dx=∫01eu du=[eu]01=e−1\int_0^1 2x\,e^{x^2}\,dx = \int_0^1 e^u\,du = \bigl[e^u\bigr]_0^1 = e - 1∫01​2xex2dx=∫01​eudu=[eu]01​=e−1
Show proof

  1. φ(x)=x2\varphi(x) = x^2φ(x)=x2 is C1C^1C1 and increasing on [0,1][0,1][0,1], with φ′(x)=2x\varphi'(x) = 2xφ′(x)=2x. The integrand 2x ex2=eφ(x) φ′(x)2x\,e^{x^2} = e^{\varphi(x)}\,\varphi'(x)2xex2=eφ(x)φ′(x) is exactly in substitution form (with f(u)=euf(u) = e^uf(u)=eu).

  2. With u=x2u = x^2u=x2 we get du=2x dxdu = 2x\,dxdu=2xdx, and the limits transform as x=0↦u=0x = 0 \mapsto u = 0x=0↦u=0, x=1↦u=1x = 1 \mapsto u = 1x=1↦u=1. Hence ∫012x ex2 dx=∫01eu du\int_0^1 2x\,e^{x^2}\,dx = \int_0^1 e^u\,du∫01​2xex2dx=∫01​eudu.

  3. Since eue^ueu is its own antiderivative, ∫01eu du=[eu]01=e−1≈1.7182818285\int_0^1 e^u\,du = [e^u]_0^1 = e - 1 \approx 1.7182818285∫01​eudu=[eu]01​=e−1≈1.7182818285. Show proof

  1. φ(x)=−x\varphi(x) = -xφ(x)=−x is C1C^1C1 and decreasing on [−1,0][-1, 0][−1,0] with φ′(x)=−1\varphi'(x) = -1φ′(x)=−1.

    Check the substitution rule's other hypothesis as well: f(u)=euf(u) = e^uf(u)=eu is continuous on every interval.

    The substitution rule gives ∫−10f(φ(x)) φ′(x) dx=∫φ(−1)φ(0)f(u) du\int_{-1}^{0} f(\varphi(x))\,\varphi'(x)\,dx = \int_{\varphi(-1)}^{\varphi(0)} f(u)\,du∫−10​f(φ(x))φ′(x)dx=∫φ(−1)φ(0)​f(u)du; with φ(−1)=1\varphi(-1) = 1φ(−1)=1 and φ(0)=0\varphi(0) = 0φ(0)=0 the right side is ∫10eu du=−∫01eu du=−(e−1)=1−e\int_{1}^{0} e^u\,du = -\int_0^1 e^u\,du = -(e - 1) = 1 - e∫10​eudu=−∫01​eudu=−(e−1)=1−e — the orientation flipped.

  2. Verify by direct computation: in ∫−10e−x⋅(−1) dx\int_{-1}^{0} e^{-x}\cdot(-1)\,dx∫−10​e−x⋅(−1)dx, −e−x-e^{-x}−e−x has antiderivative e−xe^{-x}e−x (since ddxe−x=−e−x\frac{d}{dx}e^{-x} = -e^{-x}dxd​e−x=−e−x), so the integral is [e−x]−10=e0−e1=1−e[e^{-x}]_{-1}^{0} = e^0 - e^1 = 1 - e[e−x]−10​=e0−e1=1−e. Exactly what the substitution rule predicted.
